Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe currently available orthobiologic agents, their sources, and the harvesting/processing
required for use.
Specify the mechanism of action for commonly utilized orthobiologics agents.
Identify appropriate applications for orthobiologics agents in orthopaedic practice.
Review the outcomes of orthobiologics research with regard to decision making in the clinical
setting.

Orthobiologic agents are biologically derived substances aimed at stimulating healing and
regeneration of tissues in the context of orthopaedic surgery. These tissue targets include
bone, ligaments, tendons, and muscle.
Definitions
Mesenchymal stem cells
Cells with the potential to differentiate into osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondroblasts in
vitro1
Growth factors
Signaling proteins produced by cells to induce growth of specific tissues. They can regulate
cell growth and division.
Cytokines
Proteins secreted by cells for the purpose of communication between cells or to induce a
specific reaction in the origin cell2
Osteoconduction
The process that occurs if host cells enter a scaffold that passively allows bone formation by
providing a structure for bony ingrowth and vascularization.3, 4 Osteoconduction allows for
the natural bone healing process to occur in a guided framework.
Examples
Bone autograft, bone allograft, demineralized bone matrix (DBM), calcium phosphate
Osteoinduction
The process of inducing new bone growth via externally introduced factors that cause
mesenchymal cell differentiation into the bone and chondral cells necessary for bone
formation3,5
Examples
Growth factors, bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), platelet-derived growth factor,
fibroblast growth factor, bone autograft, bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC), and
platelet-rich plasma (PRP)
Osteogenesis
The process of new bone synthesis via an introduced graft containing all the elements for
independent bone formation
Example
Cancellous bone autograft

Commonly Utilized Orthobiologic Agents
Bone Marrow Aspirate Concentrate
BMAC: autologous cell-based therapy aimed at harnessing the regenerative power of
mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), cytokines, and growth factors present in bone marrow
BMAC is harvested from the medullary canal, usually from the iliac crest.
Aspirate is then placed in a centrifuge: 60 mL of marrow aspirate yields approximately 3 to 6
mL of concentrate.
Mechanism of action: BMAC delivers growth factors (platelet-derived growth factor,
transforming growth factor-beta, BMP-2, BMP-7, interleukin-1 receptor antagonist [IL-1Ra])
and MSCs in a concentrated and localized fashion.
Origin

Origin
BMAC is harvested from the medullary canal after disruption of the cortical bone. This
procedure usually is performed under anesthesia because it requires an invasive
process. Harvest is performed with the use of an intraosseous needle, which is
introduced into the medullary canal after piercing the cortical bone with the use of a
sharp trocar or drill. The needle is used to aspirate bone marrow contents into a
heparin-loaded syringe, which prevents coagulation. These contents are then loaded
into a centrifuge for separation of cell layers, which takes 10 to 26 minutes depending
on the system.6 In most systems, 60 mL of marrow aspirate will result in
approximately 3 to 6 mL of concentrate, which is the final therapeutic product.7
Mechanism of action

Mechanism of Action
BMAC delivers MSCs and growth factors to the diseased tissue in a concentrated and
localized injection. This promotes an anabolic environment with the goal of
regenerating and repairing damaged tissue MSCs make up a small percentage of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:49 AM
AAOS | Current Applications of Orthobiologic Agents
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004076
3/18

cells in BMAC (between 0.001% to 0.01%) but remain important for their signaling
capabilities and ability to recruit local stem cells.8 The primary growth factors present
in BMAC include platelet-derived growth factor, transforming growth factor-beta,
BMP-2, BMP-7, and IL-1Ra. IL-1Ra is an inhibitor of IL-1, a cytokine implicated in the
progression of osteoarthritis. BMAC has substantially higher concentrations of IL-1Ra
than PRP.9
Platelet-Rich Plasma
PRP is an autologous blood-derived product containing bioactive molecules that facilitate
tissue repair and regeneration.
Two types of PRP preparation are commonly used in clinical practice: leukocyte-poor PRP and
leukocyte-rich PRP
There is no consensus in which type of PRP preparation is the most useful for musculoskeletal
conditions
Mechanism of action: platelets within the PRP are concentrated and contain various growth
factors that have been implicated in the healing process of various tissues

Platelet-Rich Plasma
PRP is an autologous blood-derived product containing bioactive molecules that facilitate
tissue repair and regeneration. Dissimilar from BMAC preparations, PRP is less invasive
and commonly used in the clinical setting. Autologous blood is drawn from the patient
(venipuncture) and centrifuged to concentrate platelets and remove red blood cells and
white blood cells; however, this is variable depending on the desired level of leukocytes.
Because centrifugation usually takes only 5 to 15 minutes, depending on the system that
is used, injections can be done efficiently in the same setting as the blood draw.10 The
primary mechanism of action involves platelets within the PRP that are concentrated and
contain various growth factors that have been implicated in the healing process of
various tissues. These growth factors include insulin-like growth factor-1, platelet-
derived growth factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, and transforming growth
factor-beta.11 The factors released by the activated platelets (which are stored in alpha
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:49 AM
AAOS | Current Applications of Orthobiologic Agents
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004076
4/18

granules, delta granules, or lysosomes) are thought to be responsible for the biologic
functions of PRP because of their regulatory role in tissue inflammation, cell migration
and proliferation, angiogenesis, matrix synthesis, and fibrosis.12
Two main preparations of PRP are commonly used in clinical practice: leukocyte-poor
PRP and leukocyte-rich PRP; however, no clear consensus exists with regard to which
type of PRP preparation is the most useful for musculoskeletal conditions. Some studies
have suggested that leukocyte-rich PRP is associated with a higher concentration of
proinflammatory molecules and potentiation of catabolic pathways that may negatively
affect the healing process. Contrarily, recent literature has suggested that the interaction
between leukocytes (neutrophils) and platelets in the leukocyte-rich PRP results in the
production of anti-inflammatory factors.10,12 In sports medicine, PRP injections often are
used in patients with muscle strains, tendinitis, or joint inflammation associated with
early osteoarthritis with the goal of pain mitigation and faster recovery.
Mesenchymal Stem Cells
MSCs are multipotent cells, meaning they have the potential to mature and differentiate into
different adult cell lines, including bone, cartilage, and adipose.
These cells can multiply and divide and migrate to areas at which angiogenesis is occurring.
They also exhibit the ability to activate the surrounding cells in their environment via the
release of growth factors and immune modulating factors to promote tissue proliferation.
MSCs may act as potent anti-inflammatory units.13
MSCs may be found in bone marrow, synovial tissue, periosteum, and adipose.1415
Amniotic Membrane–derived MSCs
Derived from amniotic membrane tissue, which contains higher concentrations of MSCs
compared with mature adult tissues
Origin
Cells are harvested from umbilical or placental tissue obtained from donors after
uncomplicated cesarean sections resulting in live births. Cells are then cultured and
expanded to provide additional stem cell populations for subsequent injection.16,17
Mechanism of action
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:49 AM
AAOS | Current Applications of Orthobiologic Agents
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004076
5/18

Implantation of stem cells has the potential to promote growth of new tissues, specifically
bone and cartilage, as they differentiate.
These cells may have a higher potential for osteogenic and chondral differentiation than
other types of MSCs.16
Adipose-derived stem cells
Adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (ASCs) are derived from fat tissue.
Origin
ASCs are obtained from lipoaspirate and are harvested via liposuction devices.
The cells are harvested under local anesthesia in areas such as the abdomen or flank. The
lipoaspirate is washed, processed with collagenases, and then placed into a centrifuge.
Centrifugation allows for identification and collection of the stromal vascular fraction (SVF),
which consists of stromal and vascular progenitor cells and endothelial cells. Alternative
systems may use mechanical rather than enzymatic processes to break down adipose tissue
or may use filtration rather than centrifugation to isolate the SVF.18,19
Regardless of the harvesting system, the goal components in the resultant SVF contain low
concentrations of leukocytes and extracellular matrix with no adipocytes.19 This final SVF
product may be further processed to expand ASCs in culture or may be directly injected in
single-stage procedures.20
Mechanism of action
Implantation of stem cells has the potential to promote growth of new tissues, specifically
bone and cartilage, as they differentiate. New cell growth may repair damaged tissue and
decrease inflammation and pain.13
• Bone marrow–derived stem cells
See the section on BMAC.
Hyaluronic Acid
Hyaluronic acid constitutes the viscoelastic component of the synovial fluid.21
Origin
Hyaluronic acid can be taken orally or injected.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:49 AM
AAOS | Current Applications of Orthobiologic Agents
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004076
6/18

Orthopaedic providers most commonly use hyaluronic acid as an injection in the clinic
setting for the management of joint derangements, including osteoarthritis and
inflammation.
Hyaluronic acid injections are commercially available and are derived from animal sources
(ie, rooster comb) or via modern techniques using bio-fermentation by genetically modified
organisms.22
Mechanism of action
Hyaluronic acid is a component of the extracellular matrix of the cartilage (along with
aggrecan and link protein), aiding in the formation of proteoglycan aggregate that resists
cartilage deformation via water absorption.23
Hyaluronic acid is believed to be one of the most effective intra-articular delivery systems;
therefore, it has been used in numerous studies for the development of pharmaceutical
applications (injection therapies) for the management of osteoarthritis.24
Hyaluronic acid may restore the elastoviscous properties of the synovial fluid in the short
term, promote the production of endogenous hyaluronic acid, and aid in pain reduction and
overall improvement of joint function.21,25 Hyaluronic acid has multiple pharmacologic
actions, including antioxidative and anti-inflammatory effects; reduction of pro-inflammatory
molecules; enhanced synthesis of chondrocytes; increased numbers of synovial fibroblast-
like cells; and reduction in the number of macrophages, lymphocytes, mast cells, and
adipocytes.26
Demineralized Bone Matrix
DBM is a bone graft substitute composed of allograft bone without any of the inorganic
components normally found in bone.
Origin
DBM is obtained as an allograft from cadaver donation. The bone graft is prepared via
various acidic washing techniques to remove the calcium and other inorganic components
and leave behind the organic bony elements, including collagen and growth factors.27,28
Because of the powdered nature of the final product, DBM generally is combined with
viscous biocompatible substances that allow for the formation of a putty or paste for easy
application of the product intraoperatively.27
Mechanism of action

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004076
7/18

Although the structural component of DBM is osteoconductive, it also contains signaling BMP
and vascular endothelial growth factor molecules that create an osteoinductive
environment.28 DBM may be useful as an adjunct in fracture healing after surgical
management.29
In orthopaedic surgery, the addition of DBM during surgical fracture fixation theoretically
increases healing potential.
Clinical Applications
Target Tissues
Orthobiologic use is aimed at managing multiple orthopaedic conditions, including
osteoarthritis, fracture nonunions, focal cartilage defects, tendinitis, and ligament and tendon
tears.
Basic science research shows encouraging results regarding tissue regeneration via PRP,
BMAC, and other stem cell preparations; however, clinical studies are limited.
Clinical Outcomes
BMAC
Clinical studies on the use of BMAC have shown promising results in the management of
osteoarthritis as an injectable. Centeno et al30 studied a registry of 424 arthritic joints
managed via BMAC and found substantial improvements in pain and functional outcomes with
high-dose and low-dose injections. Compared to PRP, no differences have been noted
between the two injectables; however, both treatment options have been associated with
improved patient symptoms at short-term follow-up31 (Video 1).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:49 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004076
8/18

Video 1 Stelzer, JW, Martin SD: Use of Bone Marrow Aspirate Concentrate with Hip Labral Repair
for the Management of Chondrolabral Junction Breakdown [video]. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2018. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-
page/20020__Videos. Accessed June 29, 2021.
BMAC also may aid in the process of bone healing in patients with an atrophic nonunion.
Increased progenitor cell concentrations correlate with better healing potential.3
Several small studies and case reports have shown that the addition of BMAC to a scaffold or
allograft in the management of chondral defects of the knee results in a hyaline-like cartilage
product on subsequent imaging and arthroscopy. No adverse effects were reported, showing
that BMAC is a safe treatment option for chondral defects.32
Mesenchymal Stem Cells
Some evidence shows that the injection of ASCs for the management of osteoarthritic knee
pain yields better outcome scores at short-term follow-up than a placebo.19,33,34
In a small study, injection of MSCs harvested from fat tissue were shown to decrease the size
of knee intra-articular cartilage lesions and improve patient-reported outcomes in the setting
of osteoarthritis. These results were only observed in the short term and plateaued at 2-year
follow-up35 (Video 2).

[video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020.
https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/21707__Videos. Accessed June 29, 2021.
MSCs are being used for the management of rotator cuff and Achilles tendinopathies with
promising results; however, additional studies are necessary to better quantify the positive
effects.18
Additional clinical studies on injectable MSCs are necessary.
Platelet-Rich Plasma
PRP frequently is used in the management of osteoarthritis if symptoms do not warrant
surgical management. Level I studies have shown that PRP injections can reduce pain and
improve function in patients with osteoarthritis in the knee; however, long-term follow-up is
necessary to fully understand these effects36,37 (Video 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:49 AM
AAOS | Current Applications of Orthobiologic Agents
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004076
10/18

Video 3 Jazrawi LM, Kalra K, Atanda A, Cardone DA, Hasan S: The Role of Platelet-Rich Plasma
Injection [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2012.
https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/1648__Videos. Accessed June 29, 2021.
PRP has osteoinductive properties and has been used as an adjunct in the management of
atrophic nonunions, with an 87% union rate reported by Malhotra et al.38 In the management
of long bone oligotrophic nonunions, Duramaz et al39 reported high union rates in a small
number of subjects who underwent PRP injection at the fracture site.
PRP often is combined with morselized allograft cartilage and covered with fibrin glue for the
management of articular cartilage defects. Although some promising animal studies related to
this technique have been published, no clinical trials in humans have fully elucidated the
possible benefits of this commonly used technique.32
Evidence exists for the use of PRP in the management of tendinopathy of the elbow in patients
with lateral epicondylitis. Studies have shown substantial improvement in pain after PRP
injection in patients in whom an initial 3 months of nonsurgical treatment fails.37 Some
evidence also supports the effect of PRP to be superior to corticosteroid injections for lateral
epicondylitis.40 Although the application of PRP for various tendinopathies is becoming more
common, evidence supporting the use of PRP for Achilles and rotator cuff tendinopathy
requires additional investigation.37
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004076

Although PRP has the potential to manage fracture nonunions, tendon healing, arthritic pain
relief, and cartilage defects, larger randomized studies are necessary to fully elucidate the
benefits. Lack of standardization in the preparation of PRP make the results of reported
benefits difficult to compare across studies.
Hyaluronic Acid
Hyaluronic acid improves pain and function at short-term follow-up after intra-articular
injection in the knee and hip in patients with arthritis.41,42
The indications for hyaluronic acid have been successfully expanded to other joints, including
the ankle and shoulder, with positive outcomes reported.
Whether hyaluronic acid delays the progression of disease remains unclear.22
Demineralized Bone Matrix
DBM often is combined with other biologic agents, including BMP or BMAC.
If combined with osteoinductive adjuncts, DBM results in excellent outcomes in the
management of atrophic nonunions of the tibia.
In professional football players, DBM and BMAC were a valuable adjunct to surgical fixation of
Jones fractures, resulting in a 100% rate of return to play after 8.7 weeks.3,29
Patient Considerations
Cost
The availability of orthobiologics agents in orthopaedic offices in the United States has
increased in the past decade. A recent survey of a sample size of more than 1,300 offices
found that 41.5% of the offices offered PRP injections, 20.2% of the offices offered PRP and
stem cell injections, and 1.5% of the offices offered only stem cell injections.43
Cost may be prohibitive in the use of orthobiologics agents because most insurance
companies do not cover PRP or stem cell treatments in patients with musculoskeletal
conditions. According to a report by Momaya et al,43 the mean cost of a PRP injection was
$707 (range, $175 to $4,973; standard deviation ± $388), and the mean cost of a stem cell
injection was $2,728 (range, $300 to $12,000; standard deviation ± $1584). High costs may
influence a patient’s decision regarding the use of an orthobiologic agent and, therefore, may
skew the results of outcomes because an inherent selection bias exists.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:49 AM
AAOS | Current Applications of Orthobiologic Agents
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004076
12/18

Complications of biologic agents usually are local reactions to the products themselves, which
typically are minor in nature. Similar to any invasive procedure, injections, BMAC or PRP
harvest, and surgical treatment options are associated with a small risk of infection or damage
to surrounding structures; this should always be discussed with the patient before treatment.
Most scientific studies pertaining to orthobiologics agents report no adverse events and that
these products are safe for clinical use.

Patient Considerations
Many orthobiologic agent on the market contain different combinations of factors (ie,
hyaluronic acid combined with stem cells or DBM combined with BMAC). Although their
use is becoming increasingly more prevalent, the various combinations and lack of
consistency in the numerous methods of preparation make studying these substances
difficult. Outcomes are challenging to compare because no standard preparation exists
for all the orthobiologic agent applications. Additional research and standardization are
necessary to fully understand the benefit of modern orthobiologic agents.3,18,32
Mark as Complete
